extracted.intended_audience: researchers in humor, psycholinguistics, and computational linguistics (users of lexical norms and crowd-sourced rating datasets)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and reporting a crowd-sourced dataset of humor ratings for single English words, including stimuli selection, rating procedure, participant recruitment, data trimming, aggregation (mean humor ratings), reliability checks, and demographic breakdowns. Useful for researchers building or using lexical affective norms and for computational modeling of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rated each word on a scale from 1 (humorless) to 5 (humorous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremes labeled 'humorless = not funny at all' (1) and 'humorous = most funny' (5). The middle (3) corresponds to neutral (neither humorous nor humorless). Participants were told to base ratings on first/immediate reaction and not to spend too much time thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimuli selection (word pool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words were chosen from the intersection of existing lexical norms: valence/arousal/dominance, age of acquisition, lexical decision norms, and frequency norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection produced 7,775 words; a random sample of 5,000 words was drawn to increase the number of raters per word given fixed participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calibrator words
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleven calibrator words spanning the range of humor (from pilot data) were presented first to participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrators were shown to demonstrate the range of the humor scale and increase reliability of subsequent ratings; calibrator distributions were analyzed and presented (Fig. 2, Table 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-participant stimulus protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant saw 211 words: the 11 calibrator words followed by 200 randomly sampled words (different for each participant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After selecting a rating for a word the word disappeared; sample of 200 words generated in real time when participant opened the questionnaire; participants instructed to work at a rapid pace and use first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions wording for rating
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were instructed: 'You will rate how you felt while reading each word... The rating scale ranges from 1 (humorless) to 5 (humorous).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions gave examples of what 'humorous' might mean (e.g., absurd, amusing, hilarious, playful, silly, whimsical, or laughable) and asked participants to base ratings on their immediate reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant recruitment and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk; any registered MTurk member could participate with the requirements of fully completing the study and doing it only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants paid US$1; study took approximately 15 minutes including instructions and debrief; upon accepting the HIT participants were redirected to the rating website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion / exclusion criteria (data trimming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusions included incomplete submissions, data errors/improper submissions, participants with low variability (SD of humor ratings < 0.2), and participants whose primary language was not English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial sample of 950 reduced to final 821 after removals (102 incomplete/errors, 5 low variability, 22 non-English). Partial data were not recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum and typical number of raters per word
rubrics_metrics.description: Each word was rated by at least 15 participants; the average number of participants rating a word was ~33 (M = 32.93, SD = 5.64).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures sufficient sample to compute stable mean humor ratings across 4,997 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation metric: Mean Humor Rating (MHR)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each word, all humor ratings were summed and divided by the number of participants rating the word to produce a Mean Humor Rating (MHR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MHR is the primary dependent variable provided in the dataset and used for subsequent analyses (also computed separately by demographic groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-word supplementary statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: For each word the dataset includes mean, standard deviation, and number of participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are provided for all participants combined and separately for male, female, younger, and older groups (mean_ALL, sd_ALL, n_ALL, mean_M, sd_M, n_M, etc.). File is alphabetically organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability assessment (split-half)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split-half reliability of individual ratings was computed; reported split-half reliability = 0.64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors compare this to previous similar norms (e.g., arousal ratings 0.69) and note that 0.64 indicates considerable individual differences in humor ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic breakdown and groupwise analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide and analyze MHR separately by gender (male/female) and by age (median split younger ≤32 vs older >32), and report demographic distributions (age, gender, education).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute correlations and identify words with largest gender differences (MHRM – MHRF) and age differences (MHRY – MHRO); supply separate mean/sd/n for each subgroup for further analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation with existing lexical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute correlations between Mean Humor Rating and other lexical metrics (age of acquisition, word length, frequency [BNC, SUBTLEX], lexicality RT, valence, arousal, dominance, concreteness, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report strongest correlation with frequency (less frequent words rated more humorous) and with longer lexical decision RTs; Table 5 lists pairwise correlations and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of distributional properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Report distributional statistics of MHR across words (mean, SD, skew, kurtosis, min, max) and visualize distributions (e.g., histogram Fig. 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note MHR distribution is positively skewed (more words rated as humorless than humorous) and discuss contrasts with valence norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of extreme and agreement/disagreement words
rubrics_metrics.description: List words with most extreme mean humor ratings (most humorous and most humorless) and words with largest gender/age disagreements and highest agreement subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors provide tables (Tables 4, 6, 7, 8) and visual plots (e.g., M vs F scatter with absolute gender difference labeled >1.25). They note arbitrary thresholds (e.g., 5% lowest disagreement) and encourage readers to choose their own criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization of per-participant word selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant received a different random sample of 200 words (in addition to the 11 calibrators), generated in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random sampling increases coverage while enabling multiple independent ratings per word across participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interface requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Display each word with five buttons labeled 1–5 below it; after selecting a rating the word disappears; a Submit button at the end sends responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First 11 words are calibrators shown first. UI design supports rapid first-impression ratings and prevents re-rating the same word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data availability / documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the full dataset freely available with documentation: MHRs, sd, counts, and subgroup columns, downloadable as a .csv from a public repository (GitHub).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors provide repository URL and describe the sheet organization; encourage reuse for machine learning, psychological experiments, text analysis, and stimuli creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive recommendations and suggested future uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MHRs to explore relationships between single-word humor and joke-level humor, to build machine learning predictors of word-level humor, and to study individual differences in humor styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors identify three fields of interest (linking to joke databases, ML predictors, individual differences) and suggest the norms may aid text analysis and stimulus creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment/time expectations as study design consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Set compensation and expected completion time (US$1; ~15 minutes including instructions/debrief) for crowd-sourced participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation and time estimate are reported as part of recruitment/reporting transparency and affect participant motivation and data quality.
